analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover COVID-19 diagnostic tests with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend existing health insurance rules so that group plans and individual insurers must cover tests for diagnosing COVID-19 at no cost to the patient, with no copays, deductibles, or other cost sharing. It was introduced on March 10, 2020, the early weeks of the US coronavirus outbreak, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it stalled. Days after it was introduced, Congress enacted the same free-testing requirement through other pandemic legislation, so patients got this coverage regardless.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone covered by employer group health plans or individual insurance who needed a COVID-19 test, especially people who might otherwise put off getting tested because of a copay or unmet deductible. Wider testing also slows spread, which benefits everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Adds COVID-19 diagnostic tests to the list of preventive services that health plans must cover without cost sharing, so patients pay nothing out of pocket for a test [S2][S3].
Clarifies that the plan-year interval limits normally applied to preventive service coverage do not restrict COVID-19 testing, so patients are not limited in how many tests are covered [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans bear the cost of free testing, which may be reflected somewhat in premiums. The bill does nothing for uninsured people.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises costs for insurers and employer plans, which can flow back into premiums paid by all policyholders [S3].
The bill only requires free diagnostic testing; it does not cover treatment, and it does nothing for the uninsured, who have no plan to mandate coverage through [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing a financial barrier to getting tested during a fast-spreading pandemic — was large and immediate, and the cost to insurers was comparatively modest for a single category of service. The main honest objection is that mandated free coverage adds a small amount to everyone's premiums, and that the bill left the uninsured uncovered. On balance it was a well-targeted, if narrow, consumer protection; in practice the same requirement was enacted days later in broader pandemic legislation, making this bill redundant.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; Congress enacted the same free-testing requirement in other pandemic legislation days later, so the outcome was moot.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado introduced the bill in the House on March 10, 2020, joined by Rep. Donna Shalala as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
The bill would require group health plans and insurers offering group or individual coverage to cover COVID-19 diagnostic tests without any cost sharing [S2][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on March 10, 2020, and no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insured patients did not lose out: the same no-cost-sharing requirement for COVID-19 tests became federal law eight days later in the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, so this bill's passage was unnecessary. The committee's inaction cost no one anything in the end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody lost; the policy passed in other legislation

for.name: Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require free COVID-19 test coverage and referred it to committee [S1][S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers and group plans to pay for COVID-19 tests with no patient cost sharing, a cost they would spread through premiums. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against patients wanting free tests.
Mandated free coverage removes a financial barrier to testing, increasing demand for diagnostic lab work. More testing also serves the public goal of slowing the outbreak.
